newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Ahmanson calls attacks naive.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Ahmanson calls attacks naive.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson and Co's chairman and chief executive on Thursday said arguments being used against his company's plan to acquire Great Western Financial Corp were either "naive" or a campaign of "disinformation."

In a telephone interview, Chairman and CEO Charles Rinehart focused in particular on assertions by Great Western that Ahmanson's capital structure would be inadequate and that its banking technology was outdated.
"It's either naive or disinformation," Rinehart said.
Great Western is seeking to merge with Washington Mutual Inc, and the two have signed a definitive agreement.
"There clearly is no capital issue in terms of where we are today or what is contemplated in all of our financials," Rinehart said.
He said Ahmanson's capital-to-assets ratio would never fall below 5.3 percent, compared with a regulatory requirement of 5.0 percent.
In seeking to discredit Ahmanson, he said, his opponents were making unrealistic projections of certain trends that as a practical matter would never occur simultaneously.

Rinehart said Ahmanson switched 61 of the former First Interstate branches it acquired last year to its own proprietary system. "It went without a whisper" with no adverse impact on customers, he said.

Rinehart also asserted that in a rising interest rate environment, Washington Mutual would suffer more than Ahmanson. "We don't want to root for rising rates, but they're going to be hit a lot harder than we will," he said.
He said Washington Mutual relied more heavily on wholesale borrowings to fund the liability side of its balance sheet and the cost of those borrowings would increase with rising rates.
Rinehart also said Ahmanson only had about two to three percent of its loans at fixed rates while the percentage at Washington Mutual was about a third.

Asked about the concerns of Great Western Chief Executive John Maher -- reiterated earlier Thursday -- that Ahmanson was depending on stock buybacks and cost-cutting while the Washington Mutual case is based on growth, Rinehart responded that "revenue gains are not always in the control of the company. The cost side is."
He also said the projected earnings would be superior in an Ahmanson deal without depending on revenue growth.

Rinehart said Ahmanson's first-quarter earnings of $0.87 per share diluted, reported Tuesday, showed the company was successful in developing new products, including consumer loans, small-business loans, cash-management services and investment products.
Discussing Ahmanson's consent solicitation, Rinehart said the purpose was to give shareholders of Great Western a say in the matter and not just a yes or no vote on the deal with Washington Mutual.
Ahmanson on Wednesday said it had a majority of consents on three of its proposals. One of them would require a Great Western shareholders meeting by May 6.
